name: rust-hybrid-regime-map
title: Rust hybrid engine: regime map
lead:
A pure-Rust Haseltine-Rawlings hybrid engine is compared against plain-Python and
numba-jitted baselines across a grid of synthetic models, with fidelity to exact
Gillespie SSA checked at every grid cell. Two 2-D maps (event density x stochastic
fraction, and system size x stochastic fraction) locate the speedup contours and
the accuracy frontier so a reader can see, at a glance, where the engine is both
fast and trustworthy.

at_a_glance.role: Proof the real Rust engine runs the hybrid model as a workbench composite; ~30-50x vs plain Python.
event density x stochastic fraction: Rust/numba stays 1.3-2.6x, flat; faithful only when fully stochastic.
system size x stochastic fraction: the only >=5x cells are exactly the fidelity failures - no faithful-and-fast regime.

biological_story:
Hybrid stochastic/deterministic simulation exists because biochemical networks mix
low-copy, bursty species (genes, mRNA) with high-copy, smooth ones (abundant
proteins, metabolites). The Haseltine-Rawlings partition treats the fast/high-copy
reactions as a continuous ODE and the slow/discrete ones as exact stochastic events,
trading per-molecule noise on the continuous species for speed. The engine question
is orthogonal to the biology: can writing that partitioned simulator in pure Rust
make it fast enough to matter? The map answers that the Rust engine's advantage over
compiled Python (numba) is modest (~2x) exactly in the models that are faithful, and
only grows past 5x in large, mostly-continuous models - which are precisely the ones
where treating low-copy species deterministically makes the hybrid wrong. The speed
is in the regime you cannot trust.
question:
For what kinds of models does a pure-Rust hybrid ODE/SSA engine pay off, and
where does the hybrid partition stay accurate? The viva-hybrid trial measured a
single benchmark (Rust 2.01x vs numba -> MARGINAL); this investigation sweeps
model characteristics to map WHERE a Rust hybrid engine clears the >=5x bar AND
the hybrid approximation remains faithful to exact stochastic simulation.
hypothesis:
There is a regime - overhead-dominated models with many cheap stochastic events
and few heavy continuous reactions - where the Rust engine both clears >=5x vs
the numba baseline and stays faithful to exact SSA.

executive.what_is_this:
A regime map over model characteristics. Each grid cell runs the same synthetic
hybrid model through the Rust engine and the Python baselines (N replicates),
recording Rust-vs-numba / Rust-vs-plain speedup and hybrid-vs-exact-SSA fidelity.
The maps shade speedup, draw the >=5x and <2x contours, and mask cells where the
hybrid is not faithful.
executive.verdict:
In the swept regime (copy numbers ~10-30, event density 1-1000/min, system size
3-100, timescale separation 10x, dt 0.01), NO model regime is both >=5x faster
than the numba baseline AND faithful to exact SSA. The >=5x region (large systems,
low stochastic fraction) is exactly where the hybrid partition is inaccurate; the
faithful region (fully stochastic) is where the Rust speedup is weakest (1-3x).
Against plain Python the Rust engine is 29-52x everywhere, but numba is the honest
competitor. This generalizes the single-benchmark trial (2.01x -> MARGINAL): for
this class of hybrid models a pure-Rust engine does not clear the >=5x bar where
it is also trustworthy.
executive.verdict_detail:
event_density x stochastic_fraction (system_size=10): Rust/numba 1.3-2.6x, nearly
flat in event density; fidelity_ok only at stochastic_fraction=1.0.
system_size x stochastic_fraction (density=100): Rust/numba 10.8x at (size 100,
fraction 0.1) and 6.8x at (fraction 0.25) - the only >=5x cells - both fidelity
FAIL (worst |z| ~14-17); fully-stochastic cells are 1.0x and faithful.

decisions_needed.question: Sweep copy number / species abundance as an axis?
decisions_needed.context:
Copy numbers were held low (~10-30), a regime where deterministic treatment of
a continuous species is a poor approximation by construction. High-copy
continuous species would be well-approximated deterministically and could open a
faithful-and-fast window. Copy number is the single most likely axis to change
the verdict and was not swept - the recommended next investigation.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
A pure-Rust hybrid ODE/SSA engine beats naive Python by ~30-50x but only ~1.3-2.7x
the honest numba baseline; across the swept model regimes there is no point that is
both >=5x (vs numba) and faithful to exact SSA.
evidence_for: event_density x stochastic_fraction map: Rust/numba 1.3-2.6x, flat in event density; fidelity passes only at stochastic_fraction=1.0.
system_size x stochastic_fraction map: the only >=5x cells (size 100, fraction <=0.25) all FAIL fidelity; faithful cells (fraction 1.0) are ~1.0x.
Generalizes the single-benchmark trial: Rust 2.01x vs numba -> MARGINAL (docs/results/trial-report.md).
evidence_against: Rust is 29-52x vs plain interpreted Python everywhere - if the baseline is naive Python rather than numba, the engine is a large, unambiguous win.
key_figures: reports/regime/regime_map_system_size_x_stochastic_fraction.html (speedup over system size x stochastic fraction, with >=5x/<2x contours + fidelity mask; the >=5x region and the faithful region are disjoint)
reports/regime/regime_map_event_density_x_stochastic_fraction.html (speedup over event density x stochastic fraction, system size 10: flat, sub-3x; faithful only at stochastic_fraction=1.0)
caveats: Copy numbers held low (~10-30); the fidelity frontier is copy-number dependent and copy number was NOT swept. High-copy continuous species could open a faithful-and-fast window - the top open question.
'>=5x' is measured against the numba-jitted baseline (the fair competitor); against plain Python the engine is >=29x everywhere.
At stochastic_fraction=1.0 the hybrid reduces to the exact stochastic path, so fidelity there tests engine correctness, not the partition approximation.
Single timescale_sep (10x), dt (0.01) and t_end; timing best-of-3 x 20 seeds; fidelity N=400 per cell.

competing_frameworks.name: Language/engine is the lever (rewrite in Rust)
competing_frameworks.relation: tested-and-bounded: true vs naive Python, false vs compiled (numba) Python in the faithful regime

competing_frameworks.name: Throughput/parallelism is the lever (not per-run speed)
competing_frameworks.relation: orthogonal; not tested here - see viva-core performance investigation

studies.name: rust-engine-in-workbench
studies.title: Rust engine runs the hybrid model in the workbench
studies.question:
Does the real compiled Rust hybrid engine run a hybrid ODE/SSA model end-to-end as a
process-bigraph composite inside the vivarium-workbench, and how does its per-run speed
compare to plain Python?
studies.claim:
The Rust engine runs the bursting gene-expression benchmark as a workbench composite
(RustHybridStep bridging the real run_ir binary) and is ~30-50x faster than plain
interpreted Python per run.

studies.name: speedup-landscape
studies.title: Speedup landscape: event density x stochastic fraction
studies.question:
Across event density and stochastic fraction (system size fixed at 10), how large is
the Rust-vs-numba speedup, and where is the hybrid faithful to exact SSA?
studies.claim:
Rust/numba stays 1.3-2.6x and is nearly flat in event density; the hybrid is faithful to
exact SSA only at stochastic_fraction = 1.0 (where it is the exact path).

studies.name: regime-frontier
studies.title: Regime frontier: system size x stochastic fraction
studies.question:
Sweeping system size against stochastic fraction (density 100), is there any cell that is
both >=5x faster than numba AND faithful to exact SSA?
studies.claim:
No. The only >=5x cells are large systems at low stochastic fraction (10.8x at size 100 /
fraction 0.1; 6.8x at fraction 0.25), and both FAIL fidelity (worst |z| ~14-17). The
faithful cells (stochastic_fraction = 1.0) are ~1.0x. Fast and trustworthy are disjoint.
